Toshizō went straight back to the castle-warden's lower mansion where Kondō lay,
"So it's no lie after all—that the Shogun and the Aizu Lieutenant-General have both vanished from the castle,"
he said at Kondō's pillow.
"Aye—it seems they got clean away,"
Kondō said in a small voice. "Escaped" is hardly the word for it—and Toshizō pulled a sour face.
"Then I take the field. Let all of you stand to your posts,"

—so His Highness commanded, and no sooner had he withdrawn within than he disguised himself and, without a word to his own retainers, the Shogun and the lord fled. From the battlefield the warriors who had fought for them had not yet come home. Without one word of thanks, without so much as a look at the wounded, they fled.
(Never in all the ages was the like of it heard.)
Toshizō felt like holding his head in his hands.
But Kondō, having in the last of the Kyoto days mixed with the samurai of the various clans as a "man of politics," did not feel as Toshizō did. Dimly, he grasped something of the tide of the times.
Only, the way he grasped it was a curious one.
"Toshi, this war of ours is no ordinary war. It's a bit different,"
"Different how?"
"You wouldn't understand it,"
"And you do?"
"I do,"
The big, bony face was turned to the ceiling.
(Doesn't look like the face of a man who understands.)
Toshizō could not help being amused. Kondō's political sense was, in modern terms, about that of a country town-councilman.

The essentials a politician must have are two: to hold a philosophy, and to have the sense to judge matters within the movement of world history. When the last Tokugawa years had boiled down to their dregs, the great heads among the Satsuma and Chōshū shishi had, all of them, both these essentials.
Kondō had them not.
Had them not; yet dimly, when he called to mind the arguments of such men as Gotō Shōjirō, councillor of the Tosa clan, whom he had met often in the Kyoto days, he had the feeling that he understood.
If Kondō had had the head to put the fog in his own mind into order, he
"Toshi, that war is a war of ideas,"

—would have said. A war of ideas: which is to say, the Emperor had been taken from them by Satsuma and Chōshū. In the midst of the fighting the Satsuma-Chōshū clans had forced through their plea for the brocade banner and made their own army
the "Imperial army,"
—that, and no less.

The moment the Imperial army's flag flew over Kyoto, the one who feared it most was the Shogun Yoshinobu. He had come from the Mito Tokugawa house, the very head temple of the sonnō-jōi creed, to succeed to the Hitotsubashi house, and after that to the house of the Shogun.
"that he himself would become the rebel army,"

—was what he feared most. He thought of the historical place of Ashikaga Takauji. In the last Tokugawa years, among all lettered men, of whichever party, whether for the overthrow of the shogunate or for its support, the common ground of knowledge was the history of the Northern and Southern Courts.

It was the Mito school of history that judged Takauji, who drove out the Southern Court and set up the Ashikaga shogunate, to be the greatest traitor in all history. It was men like Tokugawa Mitsukuni of Mito who raised up from the grave Takauji's enemy Kusunoki Masashige, till then all but a nameless figure in history, and made of him the greatest loyal subject in all history. The energy of the shishi of the last Tokugawa years
lay in their will to "be Masashige,"
—and there is surely no man who gave later ages more of the energy of revolution than Masashige.
When the brocade banner flew over Kyoto, Yoshinobu thought of how his name would come down to later ages if he fought on any further.
"A second Takauji,"
—that is what it would be.

It was this consciousness that made Yoshinobu take the unexampled course of "deserting his own army." In this—that political conduct and military questions had to be thought out with such a consciousness—lies the strangeness of the last Tokugawa years.

"Toshi, this is not the age of the warring provinces. Had we been born into the world of Genki and Tenshō, the likes of you and me might have made ourselves masters of a province and castle. But now it's otherwise, it seems. That, too, is why His Highness slipped secretly out of the castle in the dead of night,"
That is why, he said; but in Kondō's head the thing sat in no fine detail.
He merely had the feeling that, somehow, he understood.
"The Shogun, then, let him be. But what of the lord of Aizu, who bolted along with him?"
"Toshi, mind your words,"

"No one's listening.—Anyway, I've fought my fill at Fushimi, along the Yodo River, at Yawata, and with these eyes I saw plainly how the men of Aizu fight. Old men, young men, striplings, samurai-rank or foot-soldier alike, the Aizu clansmen fought like warriors to the very marrow. It was magnificent—no, even talking of it here I can't help the tears coming. That is what a warrior ought to be,"
"I know,"
Kondō said heavily.
"But Toshi, in this world the more you fight, the more you turn into an Ashikaga Takauji,"
(What's he blathering about.)
Toshizō rolled his eyes wide.

"Takauji or whatever he is, I don't know him—but there must be things in a man that do not change, held up against all the ages. It's toward that unchanging, precious thing that a man lives out his life,"
"Toshi, this Takauji, you see—"
"Takauji, Takauji—but if the Shogun doesn't want to be a Takauji, why not push out to Kyoto, wrest the brocade banner from Satsuma-Chōshū hands, and make himself the Imperial army?"

"Takauji did that very thing. And yet for a hundred generations after he wore the traitor's name all the same. His Highness knows it, and that is why he slipped out of the castle. You'll not know it, Toshi, but this whole plot was fixed six hundred years ago,"
"Six hundred years ago, was it,"
Toshizō said, as if teasing.
"So we've all to act to fit some tale of the far past, is that it?"
"Just so,"
Kondō nodded heavily.
Toshizō gave a low chuckle,
"It's for all the world like talking with a goblin,"
—but he did not say it aloud, and rose in silence to his feet.
Toshizō had neither learning nor doctrine, but in the rudiments he was Kondō's better. What Kondō was saying, he understood a hundred times over. What he wanted to say was only this:
(Yoshinobu and the high officers of the shogunate, just because they have a smattering of learning, are forever winning and losing against their own consciousness.)
—that was the thing. But Toshizō had no way to put it well into words.
(Just you wait and see. I'll snatch the brocade banner from the Satsuma-Chōshū crowd and make Yoshinobu and the rest of those goblins howl.)
When he got back to the intendant's residence at Kyōbashi, Nagakura Shinpachi, captain of the Second Unit, who was standing in as corps commander, came out,
"Hijikata-san, do you know?"
—and a bold grin, in this man's way, came over his face.
"This business, you mean,"
Toshizō stuck up his thumb.
"Ah—so you knew,"
"Nagakura-kun. How are the men?"
"No great unsettlement, I think. Though five or six we took on at Fushimi went out for a stroll and never came back,"
"Set them down as Chōshū spies. It bears on the men's spirit,"

Before long an order came from Asano Mimasaka-no-kami Ujihiro, the highest officer among those left at Osaka Castle, commissioner of the army with the standing of a junior councilor, telling him to come up to the castle.
Toshizō entered the great hall within the castle. For Toshizō's rank, after all, was that of a captain of the Ōgobangumi.
Among the shogunal retainers in the castle, it was a fairly high seat.
"Is there to be some great council?"
Toshizō asked the newly-appointed infantry captain Matsudaira Tarō. With Tarō he was fated later to campaign as far as Hakodate.
"I don't know,"
Matsudaira Tarō, all smiles, was eager to hear from Toshizō about the Fushimi war.
He was well disposed toward him.

Round-faced, fair-skinned, and still young. He was a man whom Western military dress became. Born to a hatamoto house, he had early taken an interest in Dutch learning and had gone through the shogunate's Western drill as well. At Hakodate, a foreigner
"He calls to mind an army officer of the French nobility,"
—would say of him.
From among the hidebound hatamoto, young men of this kind (a new species, one might well say) were now coming forth.
"I have long heard the thunder of Master Hijikata's name,"
"Come now,"
Toshizō turned the talk aside, and after telling in detail of the Satsuma army's firearms and firing-tactics at Toba-Fushimi,
"Matsudaira-san, in time the Shinsengumi too will change over to that,"

"That's well. I'm for it. Sword and spear, let alone the matchlock and the Gewehr, are guns no longer. This is an age when breech-loading repeaters are just beginning to appear even abroad. It is weapons that decide a war,"
"Quite true,"
"Master Hijikata, might I ask your acquaintance from this chance on?"
"It is I who should wish it. By the way—have you some plain book on Western-style fighting? One I might read a single volume of and get some shape of the thing,"
"How about this?"
Matsudaira Tarō drew from his pocket a small booklet, Japanese-bound and woodblock-printed.
"Infantry Handbook,"
was the title.

It was an official infantry drill-manual issued by the shogunate's Institute of Military Science. What was marked on it as the "1860 pattern" was the Western year: it was a translation of the Dutch army's issue for the year 1860.
When Toshizō riffled through it, the names of things were in Dutch, but he could make a fair guess at them.
"Soldaat—that would be a rank-and-file man,"
"Well now, does Master Hijikata do Dutch?"
"Sheer guesswork. So then—'compagnie' seems to mean a unit. 'Onderofficier' is a samurai-rank man, and 'korporaal' a petty officer, is it?"
"You astonish me,"
"A thing like this, being kana within Japanese text, one can guess at. But this is the drill for the old-style Jäger rifle, is it not,"
"It is,"
"Aizu had those too, and got badly cut up for it—have you none for the new-model gun?"
"No; the handling of the gun differs, but the make-up of a unit does not change. So even that book will be of some use to you,"
"Well, better than nothing,"
As Toshizō was buried in his reading, Asano Mimasaka-no-kami at length appeared and began giving directions for the transport to Edo of the troops left at Osaka. Partway through,
"Hijikata-dono,"
said Mimasaka-no-kami.
Toshizō was reading the Infantry Handbook. It was hugely interesting. A book of fighting. Not once in all his years had Toshizō read a book so interesting.
"Hijikata-dono,"
said Mimasaka-no-kami a second time.
Matsudaira Tarō nudged Toshizō's knee.
(Eh?)
—with such a look, Toshizō raised his face.
"Your Shinsengumi will board the warship Fujiyama-maru, sailing on the twelfth. Muster at the Tenpōzan quay at four o'clock in the dawn of the twelfth,"
"Understood,"
He bowed his head slightly and dropped his eyes back to the Infantry Handbook.
(Splendid stuff.)
At that moment there can have been no man in the castle with a livelier look on his face.
(If it's the twelfth, there's still time.)

On horseback Toshizō turned north along the edge of the moat. To his right would be, in present-day terms, the Osaka Prefectural Office. It was all one pine wood, and a little back from it the warden's residence and other samurai mansions, great and small, stood ranged in a row.
Toshizō walked his horse northward.
The northern sky was clear to the point of pain in the eyes. That a few days before they had suffered so utter a defeat—heaven and earth made it seem a lie.
(The earth, it seems, goes turning on with no care for the affairs of men.)
Toshizō was seized, of a sudden, by a boyish sentiment. It was a habit that came out in this man now and then.
It was mostly at such times that he would twist off one of the clumsy haiku he had from his brother.
All at once a river-wind reached his nose. The Osaka intendant's residence, the Shinsengumi's quarters (near the present-day Keihan Tenma station) must be close by.
Ahead, and a little to the right, the castle gate at the Kyōbashi entrance came into view.

From about the front of that Kyōbashi entrance, running north and south, was a long embankment, grown into a wood of old pines standing close and thick, which gave the castle's northern quarter an air of great gracefulness.
Gulls were flying beyond that pine wood.
The tide seemed to be pushing up the river.
When he came as far as the pine wood,
(Ah—)
and Toshizō got down from his horse.
He was flustered to a degree he himself thought unseemly.
In the pine wood was Oyuki.
Far off.
(It cannot be.)
he thought; but taking his horse by the bridle he began to walk.
The woman, too, began to walk.
Once she had begun to walk, by the way she carried herself he knew it was Oyuki.
"You have been in Osaka, I hear,"
Toshizō meant to smile. But his heart pounded too hard for it to become a smile.
Toshizō, most likely, wore the face of a boy.
"I thought you might scold me,"
Oyuki seemed to be trying, as hard as she could, to make her face without a shadow on it.
She was smiling brightly.
But that if one so much as touched that cheek with a fingertip it would crumble—that danger, even Toshizō could feel.
"Oyuki-san, wait for me here. I will come at once,"
Toshizō galloped to the intendant's residence, only some five minutes off even on foot.
Down he sprang, and walking along the corridor,
"Officieren—officers—gather to me,"
he said.
They all looked blank. Toshizō, who had blurted it out, caught himself with a start. The words of the Infantry Handbook he had read a while before had burned themselves into his head.
"No—unit captains, inspectors, corporals,"
he said again, correcting himself, and they all gathered.
"On the twelfth we sail east on the Fujiyama-maru. Let our departure from quarters that night be at the Hour of the Ox. We rise again once we are back in the Kantō. Now then—"
and Toshizō colored in the face.
"I should like two days' leave,"
"Where will you go?"
Nagakura Shinpachi asked. And Harada Sanosuke too,
"That you should take leave—there's a rare thing,"
said in dead earnest.
"I have a woman,"

At that they were all astonished—less that Toshizō had a woman or had none than that this man, who even when he had such a thing had oddly always kept it hidden, should say it now as if throwing off all concealment.
"I have one. I think of her as my own wife, and more than that,"
"Enough said,"
Harada stopped him.
"Go. The corps' business while you're away, Nagakura and I and these men here will see to it. The real point of calling us together was that, wasn't it, rather than any Fujiyama-maru,"
"I'm in your debt,"
"It's only right. But that even you had such a woman—that is a glad thing,"
It was no sarcasm. Harada Sanosuke said it with tears starting to his eyes.
For the blood that ran in Toshizō was spoken of as a demon's, or a serpent's.
"It's made even me glad,"
and Nagakura's face broke into a grin. Both Harada and Nagakura had wives of their own. But in this upheaval of war, neither of the two so much as knew where his own wife was.
Toshizō had them all withdraw and changed his clothes. He put on a crested formal coat and Sendai-hira hakama.
In haste he left the quarters.
He went to the pine wood.
The colors of dusk were beginning to gather.
"Oyuki-dono,"
A shadow moved.
Toshizō drew her to him. Now let anyone see, and be damned to it.
"Oyuki-dono. Let us go somewhere the water and the pines are beautiful. I have taken two days' leave. There, the two of us will live together,"
"—I am happy,"
Oyuki said, in a voice almost too low to hear.
